title: Replace combinational division with one iterative divide unit
motivation:
The baseline's 199.8 ns, 156-cell critical path crosses forwarding and
the EX ALU, where the four SystemVerilog divide and remainder expressions
infer deep combinational arithmetic. Its 5.442 MHz Fmax leaves a large
opportunity: CoreMark pays for this path on every clock even though divide
instructions are relatively infrequent. The sole prior micro_opt result
is the unchanged baseline, so this path has not yet been addressed.

hypothesis.motivation:
The baseline's 199.8 ns, 156-cell critical path crosses forwarding and
the EX ALU, where the four SystemVerilog divide and remainder expressions
infer deep combinational arithmetic. Its 5.442 MHz Fmax leaves a large
opportunity: CoreMark pays for this path on every clock even though divide
instructions are relatively infrequent. The sole prior micro_opt result
is the unchanged baseline, so this path has not yet been addressed.
hypothesis.hypothesis:
Replace the four combinational DIV/DIVU/REM/REMU datapaths with one shared,
radix-16 restoring unsigned divider in EX. Unroll four quotient bits per
clock to finish a general 32-bit operation in eight clocks. Capture
forwarded operands when a divide starts, convert signed operands to
magnitudes for DIV/REM, then
correct quotient and remainder signs per RV32M. Handle divide by zero and
INT_MIN / -1 explicitly. Hold IF and ID/EX while the unit runs, let the
older EX/MEM instruction drain exactly once, inject bubbles into EX/MEM
until the result is ready, and issue the divide result exactly once on the
eighth step, without a separate completion bubble. This bounds the gap
between back-to-back retirements for the deep-formal liveness window. Give
an outstanding dmem stall priority over divider launch and completion.
Preserve the existing RISCV_FORMAL_ALTOPS combinational substitutes for
fast formal checks. This local arithmetic change should exchange a small
number of extra divide cycles for a much shorter clock period and a large
reduction in divide logic area.

Wire divider hold and completion into the existing pipeline controls without changing the top-level ports or retirement order.

Keep exact RV32M arithmetic vectors and adapt divide cases to the new clocked result handshake, including back-to-back operations and corner cases.
Exercise division after forwarded operands and adjacent divides under imem/dmem stalls; check single retirement, RVFI data, and forward progress.

title: Replace combinational division with a shared radix-4 divider
motivation:
The baseline's 199.837 ns, 156-cell critical path passes through EX and the
ALU, where four combinational DIV/REM expressions create a deep divider
cone. Fmax is only 5.442 MHz, so shortening that path should be worth far
more than the extra cycles spent on the relatively infrequent divisions in
CoreMark. A single iterative unit should also reduce LUT use.

hypothesis.motivation:
The baseline's 199.837 ns, 156-cell critical path passes through EX and the
ALU, where four combinational DIV/REM expressions create a deep divider
cone. Fmax is only 5.442 MHz, so shortening that path should be worth far
more than the extra cycles spent on the relatively infrequent divisions in
CoreMark. A single iterative unit should also reduce LUT use.
hypothesis.hypothesis:
Implement one shared radix-4 unsigned restoring divider for DIV, DIVU, REM,
and REMU. Latch the forwarded operands and operation when a valid divide
reaches EX; convert signed operands to unsigned magnitudes, produce two
quotient bits per cycle, and correct quotient or remainder sign at the end.
Complete every divide within 16 iteration cycles plus at most two control
cycles, including divide-by-zero and INT_MIN/-1 semantics. Hold IF and ID/EX
while the divide is pending, let older EX/MEM and MEM/WB work drain, inject
EX/MEM bubbles during iteration, and emit the divide result into EX/MEM
exactly once when ready. Existing dmem stalls take priority before launch
and at completion. Keep the ALTOPS arithmetic substitution at the same
divider completion point so formal checks exercise the multicycle control
path. The shorter EX path should raise Fmax enough to overcome the added
divide latency without changing the single-retire or memory contracts.

title: Predict branch direction during instruction fetch
motivation:
The baseline fetches PC+4 until a branch resolves in EX, so every taken
conditional branch discards the following fetch. CoreMark has frequent loop
branches, and instruction-bus stalls amplify the cost of fetching the wrong
path. A small direction predictor can remove this bubble on correctly
predicted branches without changing the RV32IM retirement contract.

hypothesis.motivation:
The baseline fetches PC+4 until a branch resolves in EX, so every taken
conditional branch discards the following fetch. CoreMark has frequent loop
branches, and instruction-bus stalls amplify the cost of fetching the wrong
path. A small direction predictor can remove this bubble on correctly
predicted branches without changing the RV32IM retirement contract.
hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add a 64-entry, two-bit saturating branch-history table indexed by fetch PC.
On the first encounter of an entry, predict backward conditional branches
taken and forward conditional branches not taken; subsequently use the
counter's high bit. In IF, form the B-immediate target from the fetched
instruction and select it as the next fetch PC only when a legal branch
funct3 is recognized, the target is aligned and within the mapped instruction
memory range, the bus is ready, and the branch is predicted taken. Carry the
predicted next PC and prediction-valid bit
through ID/EX. In EX, compare the actual next PC with the predicted next PC,
redirect and squash the younger instruction only on a mismatch, and update
the counter once per resolved branch. Keep direct JAL on the existing EX
redirect path to limit this experiment to conditional branch prediction.
Prediction state changes only for a valid conditional branch advancing past
EX, and neither an instruction-bus stall nor a data-bus stall may consume a
prediction or train the table twice. Misaligned taken targets must retain the existing
trap behavior and use PC+4 as the actual next PC. RVFI reports the resolved
next PC, independent of the speculative fetch path.

Resolve the actual branch next PC, redirect only on misprediction, and issue one branch-history update per advancing branch.
Connect the branch-history table, fetch prediction, EX resolution, and stall-qualified update signals.
Squash IF and ID only on a true EX redirect while preserving branch and prediction state across data-bus stalls.
Implement a compact 64-entry two-bit direction table with cold-entry backward-taken bias and reset state.
Exercise repeated taken and untaken branches, table aliasing, wrong-path recovery, and simultaneous instruction/data bus stalls.

title: Shorten branch redirect feedback into decode
motivation:
The radix-4 divider champion reaches 47.41 MHz, but its worst 27.233 ns path
starts at the register file, crosses EX branch resolution, then passes through
IF instruction masking and ID hazard/decode logic before reaching ID/EX.
CoreMark took the same 4,491,485 cycles after the divider change, so Fmax is
the immediate opportunity. The earlier branch predictor improved cycles but
retained the deep arithmetic path and scored below this champion.

hypothesis.motivation:
The radix-4 divider champion reaches 47.41 MHz, but its worst 27.233 ns path
starts at the register file, crosses EX branch resolution, then passes through
IF instruction masking and ID hazard/decode logic before reaching ID/EX.
CoreMark took the same 4,491,485 cycles after the divider change, so Fmax is
the immediate opportunity. The earlier branch predictor improved cycles but
retained the deep arithmetic path and scored below this champion.
hypothesis.hypothesis:
Break the combinational redirect-to-instruction-to-hazard path while keeping
branch resolution in EX. IF should carry the fetched instruction unchanged
and mark it invalid during redirect or instruction-bus stall. ID should turn
invalid fetches into control-zero bubbles at its register boundary; decoder
legality still defaults to illegal for every actual instruction. Qualify
load-use detection with instruction-bus readiness and use the raw fetched
source fields, allowing redirect to drive only the direct ID flush and PC
selection paths. Also share equality and unsigned less-than results for all
six branch conditions, deriving signed less-than from operand sign bits, to
shorten and reduce the EX comparison cone. Preserve redirect priority over
stalls, precise traps, single retirement, and all RVFI fields. A reduction
of several logic levels on the reported worst path should raise median Fmax
enough to exceed the 4.6% acceptance threshold with little cycle impact.

Qualify load-use checks with imem readiness and keep redirect as a direct flush/PC signal, independent of fetched instruction bits.
Use shared equality and unsigned comparison with sign-bit correction for signed branch conditions; preserve misalignment traps and resolved PC reporting.
Exercise taken branches and jumps across load-use, imem stalls, and dmem stalls; check wrong-path suppression, retirement order, and RVFI next PCs.

lesson: - 2026-09-28 hyp-20260928-001-r2s0 (improvement, +17.25%): With combinational IF/ID, masking fetched instructions on EX redirect extends branch resolution through decode and load-use logic into ID/EX timing; passing raw fetch data and flushing ID/EX validity, alongside registering MUL products, shortened the timed logic and raised fitness.

title: Decouple ID/EX data storage from bubble control
motivation:
The champion's 27.233 ns worst path starts at the register file, passes through
EX branch resolution, IF redirect and hazard logic, and ends at an ID/EX rs2
operand flop. The ID stage currently clears its entire wide pipeline bundle
on a redirect or load-use bubble, so a branch decision is on the D path of
operand and instruction data that do not need to be zeroed. This path limits
Fmax even though CoreMark throughput already holds at 4,491,485 cycles.

hypothesis.motivation:
The champion's 27.233 ns worst path starts at the register file, passes through
EX branch resolution, IF redirect and hazard logic, and ends at an ID/EX rs2
operand flop. The ID stage currently clears its entire wide pipeline bundle
on a redirect or load-use bubble, so a branch decision is on the D path of
operand and instruction data that do not need to be zeroed. This path limits
Fmax even though CoreMark throughput already holds at 4,491,485 cycles.
hypothesis.hypothesis:
Split ID/EX into wide data registers and a narrow valid/control register.
Hold the data registers only while a dmem stall or an in-flight divide needs
the current EX instruction preserved; let them capture freely during a
redirect or load-use bubble. On redirect, load-use, or unavailable
instruction memory, clear ID/EX valid and side-effect control instead of
clearing the wide operand, immediate, PC, register-address and instruction
fields. Keep dmem/divide hold priority over bubble insertion.
Keep the raw imem instruction on IF's data path and carry fetch validity
separately; gate load-use detection with fetch validity. Ensure invalid
ID/EX entries have zero side-effect controls so they cannot redirect,
access memory, write a register, launch division, or retire. Preserve
existing dmem-stall priority and the nret=1 RVFI contract. This removes
the EX-to-IF-to-ID control feedback from wide register D muxes and should
increase Fmax with unchanged instruction count and branch penalty.

title: Tagged target predictor with registered branch recovery
motivation:
The current core waits until EX to redirect every taken branch and jump,
discarding two younger fetches. An earlier fetch-stage direction predictor
reduced CoreMark cycles by 5.4%, but it was measured before the divider
change, when a 198 ns arithmetic path hid predictor timing. The present
27.2 ns worst path runs through EX branch resolution, IF redirect, and ID
control; adding an EX-to-IF misprediction comparator directly to that path
would risk losing the IPC gain through lower Fmax.

hypothesis.motivation:
The current core waits until EX to redirect every taken branch and jump,
discarding two younger fetches. An earlier fetch-stage direction predictor
reduced CoreMark cycles by 5.4%, but it was measured before the divider
change, when a 198 ns arithmetic path hid predictor timing. The present
27.2 ns worst path runs through EX branch resolution, IF redirect, and ID
control; adding an EX-to-IF misprediction comparator directly to that path
would risk losing the IPC gain through lower Fmax.
hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add a 32-entry, direct-mapped, full-PC-tagged branch-target buffer that predicts the
complete next PC in IF without decoding the fetched instruction or adding
its immediate on the fetch-to-PC path. Store resolved targets for conditional
branches, JAL, and JALR. Use a two-bit saturating counter for conditional
direction, always predict a tagged JAL entry taken, and predict a JALR target
only after the same target has been observed twice at that site. Carry the
predicted next PC with each instruction. Resolve the actual next PC in EX
as before, but register both actual and predicted PCs into EX/MEM and perform
misprediction recovery from that register in MEM. This removes the forwarded
register-file/branch-compare path from the redirect feedback loop, while
warm loop branches and direct jumps can proceed without fetch bubbles.
On recovery, redirect the PC and kill every younger IF, ID, and EX payload
before any wrong-path memory access or retirement. Train the buffer exactly
once when the resolving instruction advances through MEM; never train on a
stalled or squashed instruction. A BTB miss follows PC+4. A stale prediction,
changed instruction, misaligned target, or tag alias is corrected by the
full actual-versus-predicted PC comparison. Reset table valid bits so target
payload can infer distributed RAM. Preserve the resolved RVFI next PC, trap
behavior, nret=1 ports, and bus-stall semantics.

Carry predicted next PC through IF/ID, ID/EX, and EX/MEM, and retain control-flow type and resolved outcome for MEM recovery and training.

Check warm branch and jump predictions, tag aliases, stale instruction recovery, and recovery during instruction/data stalls with exact RVFI order.

title: Shorten the EX memory-address datapath
motivation:
The champion's 23.099 ns worst path starts in the register file and runs
through EX forwarding and the general ALU to the data-memory address.
Loads and stores need only forwarded rs1 plus their immediate, but their
address currently traverses the ALU operand selection and multi-operation
result mux. CoreMark's cycle count is already near the earlier nonpredictive
designs, so shortening this frequent timed path is the best micro-opt
opportunity. Prior micro_opt attempts addressed division, not this path.

hypothesis.motivation:
The champion's 23.099 ns worst path starts in the register file and runs
through EX forwarding and the general ALU to the data-memory address.
Loads and stores need only forwarded rs1 plus their immediate, but their
address currently traverses the ALU operand selection and multi-operation
result mux. CoreMark's cycle count is already near the earlier nonpredictive
designs, so shortening this frequent timed path is the best micro-opt
opportunity. Prior micro_opt attempts addressed division, not this path.
hypothesis.hypothesis:
Give valid LOAD and STORE instructions a dedicated EX effective-address
calculation from forwarded rs1 and the decoded immediate. Register this
sum with the existing EX/MEM advance and hold behavior, and use it for the
dmem address, byte-lane selection, alignment checks, and RVFI memory
address. Keep the general ALU result path for nonmemory instructions and
preserve all forwarding, bus-stall, misalignment-trap, and retirement
semantics. Structure the address path so the general ALU operation decode
and result mux are absent between forwarded rs1 and the registered memory
address. This should remove several LUT levels from the measured critical
path without adding cycles; a clock increase above about 5% would clear
the champion's acceptance threshold at similar CoreMark IPC.

title: Separate load/store address generation from the shared EX ALU
motivation:
The current champion reaches 56.756 MHz, and its worst timed path runs
from the register file through EX and the shared ALU into data memory.
An earlier structural change shortened branch feedback but exposed this
same address path and reduced fitness. Every load and store currently
pays for the general ALU operand and result selection even though its
effective address is always forwarded rs1 plus the decoded immediate.

hypothesis.motivation:
The current champion reaches 56.756 MHz, and its worst timed path runs
from the register file through EX and the shared ALU into data memory.
An earlier structural change shortened branch feedback but exposed this
same address path and reduced fitness. Every load and store currently
pays for the general ALU operand and result selection even though its
effective address is always forwarded rs1 plus the decoded immediate.
hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add a dedicated 32-bit base-plus-offset address generator beside the EX
ALU. Calculate the load/store effective address directly from the
forwarded rs1 value and immediate, and capture it in a separate EX/MEM
register. Drive the dmem address, byte alignment checks, lane masks,
load extraction, and RVFI memory address from that registered address.
Keep the general ALU result register for arithmetic, jumps, and writeback;
loads use memory data for writeback and stores have no writeback, so their
ALU result need not feed the timed memory address path. Preserve forwarding
precedence, dmem holds, misalignment traps, single retirement, and the
existing RV32M and ALTOPS behavior. This should remove the ALU operation
mux and unrelated arithmetic from the load/store address cone without
adding a cycle to the pipeline.

title: Predict direct control flow with compact branch history
motivation:
The current fetch PC advances by four until EX resolves a taken branch or
jump. CoreMark pays a wrong-path bubble for common loop branches. A previous
32-entry tagged target buffer saved about 6.6% of cycles but lowered Fmax
from 56.8 to 49.7 MHz, so it lost fitness. Its target storage, tags, full
next-PC comparison, and MEM-stage recovery added circuit cost that a direct
branch or JAL does not need.

hypothesis.motivation:
The current fetch PC advances by four until EX resolves a taken branch or
jump. CoreMark pays a wrong-path bubble for common loop branches. A previous
32-entry tagged target buffer saved about 6.6% of cycles but lowered Fmax
from 56.8 to 49.7 MHz, so it lost fitness. Its target storage, tags, full
next-PC comparison, and MEM-stage recovery added circuit cost that a direct
branch or JAL does not need.
hypothesis.hypothesis:
Predict conditional branch direction in IF using a 64-entry two-bit
saturating history table indexed by fetch PC. Use backward-taken and
forward-not-taken as the cold-entry choice, and predict aligned direct JAL
targets unconditionally. Decode only the branch/JAL opcode and valid branch
funct3 in IF; form their immediate targets from the fetched instruction.
Do not add a BTB, full-PC tags, or a target array. Carry only a predicted-
taken bit with the instruction into ID/EX. In EX, compare that bit with the
resolved branch outcome and redirect only when the direction was wrong;
an unpredicted JALR retains the existing redirect. A mispredicted taken
branch redirects to its resolved target, and a mispredicted not-taken
branch redirects to PC+4. The existing EX branch comparison and ALU-to-dmem
datapaths stay unchanged. Train each conditional branch exactly once when
its valid EX result advances; never train on a held or squashed instruction.
Fetch prediction applies only when imem is ready and the target is aligned;
EX retains authority for traps, recovery, and the RVFI next PC. Redirect
retains priority over bus stalls. This should recapture most of the BTB's
cycle saving while preserving enough of the champion's Fmax to clear the
4.6% fitness threshold.

changes.description: Add a small two-bit direction table with cold backward-taken bias, combinational lookup, and stall-qualified EX training.
Recognize valid direct branches and JAL, form aligned immediate targets, select predicted fetch PC, and give EX recovery priority over stalls.
Carry one predicted-taken bit in IF/ID and ID/EX payloads without widening the EX/MEM or MEM/WB datapaths.
Latch the prediction bit with each valid instruction and clear it on a flush or invalid fetch.
Redirect conditional branches only on a direction mismatch, leave JALR resolution in EX, and expose branch outcome for training.
Connect IF lookup and EX training with qualification for stalls, flushes, and valid instructions.
Preserve exactly one younger-instruction squash on EX misprediction and the current bus-stall priorities.
